How the 12 weeks work

Two full-body team sessions a week, on the same two days all winter. Learn runs Weeks 1–2, Build Weeks 3–8 and Apply Weeks 9–12, and each phase builds on the last. We test in Weeks 1, 6 and 12. Growth is measured from Week 1 to Week 12; Week 6 is a mid-point check-in.

Every session, same shape

Speed always comes first, while legs are fresh. If you only have 60 minutes, trim the strength circuit to one round and the game to 8 minutes. Never cut the warm-up or the game.

Know before Week 1

No throwing until FebruaryPitch Smart calls for 2–3 months in a row off. That's November through January. Combine DaySix quick tests in Weeks 1, 6 and 12. No lasers or radar gun needed. Seadogs Combine CupTeam points for effort, sportsmanship and beating your Week 1 numbers. Coach safety rulesSupervision, growth-spurt knee and heel pain, multi-sport kids.

12-minute warm-up

The same warm-up starts every session: Raise, Activate, Mobilize, Potentiate. It follows the FIFA 11+ Kids approach of balance, landing and strength. In soccer, that approach cut injuries by about half.

Tank rules

    Combine Day testing

    We test in Weeks 1, 6 and 12. The only growth we track is each kid's change from Week 1 to Week 12. Week 6 is a mid-point check-in so kids and coaches can see they are on track. Share each kid's progress with them, and keep raw rankings private to coaches.

    Same everything, every time

    • Same turf, same shoes, same time of day.
    • Same warm-up, plus 2 practice reps.
    • Same timer. One adult times every kid.
    • Measure height (shoes off, against a wall) on every test day.

    Timing without lasers

    1. Phone slow-motion video (240 frames/second), filmed from the side at the finish line. Count frames from the first movement to the torso crossing the line. Free and far more consistent than a thumb on a stopwatch.
    2. Stopwatch: the same adult times every kid, starts on the athlete's first movement (no "Go!"), and records the best of 2 with 2–3 minutes' rest.

    The six tests

    Growth spurts change results. A kid who grows a couple of inches over the winter may jump the same or run slower in Week 6 or Week 12. That's normal. Compare each kid to their own Week 1 result, and race kids against others their size.

    Games & the Combine Cup

    Kids quit when it stops being fun or they feel "not good enough". Competition works when every kid has a real chance, so the points reward improvement, effort and sportsmanship alongside speed.

    Seadogs Combine Cup

    Coaches draft balanced teams that mix ages, sizes and maturity. Keep teams for 4 weeks, then redraft. Leaderboards show improvement from Week 1 to Week 12 ("Most inches added", "Most tests improved"), never raw rank. Raw scores go privately to each family.

    Speed & Power Card

    Each kid keeps a card. Badges come from beating their own Week 1 numbers in Week 12, so a late bloomer can earn gold.

    BronzeBeat Week 1 in any 2 tests
    SilverBeat Week 1 in any 3 tests
    GoldBeat Week 1 in 4 or more tests

    A test skipped for a growth-related ache doesn't count against a kid.

    Arm care

    USA Baseball and MLB's Pitch Smart guidance for ages 9–12 is clear about rest. This program builds the arm without throwing it.

    Pitch Smart, ages 9–12

      The Seadogs window

      Arm care in this program

      A selection from the Youth Thrower's Ten, a published routine for young throwers. Use a light band, 1–2 sets of 10, twice a week, inside the strength block.

      After pitching (spring handout)

      For the spring season. Hand this to families when kids start pitching again.

        Red flags.

        Fuel & water

        Simple and kid-sized. For 9–12 year olds, the American Academy of Pediatrics suggests about 3–8 oz of water every 20 minutes.

        No weigh-ins, no body-weight talk, and no "good" or "bad" food language with this age group.

        Coaching & safety

        For volunteer coaches. Youth strength and power training is safe when it is supervised, technique comes first, and it progresses step by step.

        This guide is general training information, not medical advice. If a child has pain that lasts or keeps coming back, check with a doctor or physical therapist.
